item.title: Should space data centers run on solar panels, nuclear reactors or both?
item.description: The last few days we've been covering a series of papers by Dr. Slava Turyshev of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory about the constraints surrounding the use of orbital data centers in space. One that has come up repeatedly is weight, and the solar panels used to power these data centers contribute a significant portion of that weight. So why not go with an alternative power source? Nuclear energy in space applications is having a bit of a moment currently—maybe it could provide the power needed for the orbital data center revolution? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI simulates electron hops over far longer times than conventional quantum calculations
item.description: To predict how a material will behave, we need to know which atoms are located where. This allows us, for example, to explain whether a material is suitable as a catalyst for certain chemical reactions. But often, that is not enough: even if all the atoms stay exactly where they are, the distribution of electric charge within the material can change dramatically. Electrons can jump from one atom to another, changing the forces between atoms as well as the material's chemical reactivity. Fuente: Phys.org.

The calculations suggest that this allows CO₂ to be converted preferentially into formic acid. The findings have been published in Advanced Functional Materials. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: ATLAS finds hints of the hidden structure of the vacuum
item.description: Researchers at the University of Bonn, together with colleagues from Oxford and Prague, played a leading role in analyzing particle collisions at CERN's Large Hadron Collider. The ATLAS Collaboration observed more proton collisions with the particle pattern it was looking for than expected. This could point to a phenomenon predicted by the Standard Model of particle physics that has never been directly observed, known as QCD instanton processes. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ozone hole one of the largest in decades
item.description: In contrast to the 2025 seasonal ozone hole above Antarctica, which was the fifth smallest since 1992, this year's ozone hole ranks as one of the largest in 48 years, based on long-term atmospheric observations, including data from the Copernicus Sentinel-5P satellite. While this may sound alarming, it is important to remember that the size of the ozone hole varies naturally from year to year, and the long-term recovery of the ozone layer remains on track. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The dark matter puzzle deepens: Nearby galaxies challenge cosmic simulations
item.description: Galaxies appear to hold a surprise beneath their visible stars: Their inner regions contain less dark matter than some of our most advanced simulations predict. Dark matter is invisible, but its gravitational pull helps govern the motions of stars and gas. By measuring these movements, astronomers can reconstruct where this unseen matter lies and test the computer simulations used to understand the universe. A study of 136 nearby galaxies, involving the Instituto de Astrofísica de Canarias (IAC), reveals a discrepancy that becomes more extensive in more massive systems, offering fresh clues… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why fertile male killifish outlive their peers
item.description: Why do some individuals of the same species live significantly longer than others? In evolutionary biology and aging research, this question is often linked to a trade-off between reproduction and survival. The underlying idea is that energy and resources invested in reproduction may lead to compromises in repair and maintenance, thereby hindering a long life. Thus, the assumption is that particularly successful reproduction at a young age comes at the cost of a shorter lifespan. Fuente: Phys.org.
